facts.value: Research published in 2015 suggests that incorporating mindfulness into physical exercise interventions increases exercise adherence and self-efficacy, and also has positive effects both psychologically and physiologically.
Exercising looks different in every country, as do the motivations behind exercising.
In some countries, people exercise primarily indoors (such as at home or health clubs), while in others, people primarily exercise outdoors.
People may exercise for personal enjoyment, health and well-being, social interactions, competition or training.
In Colombia, citizens value and celebrate the outdoor environments of their country, using outdoor activities as social gatherings to enjoy nature and their communities.
In Bogotá, Colombia, a 70-mile stretch of road known as the Ciclovía is shut down each Sunday for bicyclists, runners, rollerbladers, skateboarders and other exercisers.
In Cambodia, public gyms have become quite popular, where people congregate to use the facilities as well as organize aerobics and dance sessions open to the public.
Sweden has begun developing outdoor gyms, called utegym, which are free to the public and often placed in beautiful environments.
In some areas of China, particularly among retired individuals, morning square dances are held in public parks, allowing for both health and social benefits.
These sociocultural variations in physical exercise show how different geographic locations and social climates influence motivations and methods of exercising.
Adhering or staying consistent with an exercise program can be challenging for many people.

Many different factors can affect adherence such as why a person is exercising (e.g, health, social), types of exercises or how the exercise program is structured, involvement of professionals in the program, education related to exercise and health, monitoring and progress made in the exercise program, goal setting, and involvement in choosing the exercise program and setting goals.
Proper nutrition is as important to health as exercise.
It is important to have a good diet to ensure that the body has the correct ratio of macronutrients while providing ample micronutrients to aid recovery following strenuous exercise.
Active recovery is recommended after participating in physical exercise because it removes lactate from the blood more quickly than inactive recovery.
Removing lactate from circulation allows for an easy decline in body temperature, which can benefit the immune system.
Exercise physiologists recommend the '4-Rs framework': Rehydration, Refuel, Repair, Rest.
Replacing any fluid and electrolyte deficits.
Consuming carbohydrates to replenish muscle and liver glycogen.
Consuming high-quality protein sources with additional supplementation of creatine monohydrate.
Getting long and high-quality sleep after exercise, additionally improved by consuming casein proteins, antioxidant-rich fruits, and high-glycemic-index meals.
Exercise has an effect on appetite, but whether it increases or decreases appetite varies from individual to individual, and is affected by the intensity and duration of the exercise.
Overtraining occurs when a person exceeds their body's ability to recover from strenuous exercise.

Overtraining can be described as a point at which a person may have a decrease in performance or plateau as a result of failure to perform at a certain level or training-load consistently; a load which exceeds their recovery capacity.
People who are overtrained cease making progress, and can even begin to lose strength and fitness.
Overtraining is also known as chronic fatigue, burnout, and overstress in athletes.
Monotonous program overtraining suggests that repetition of the same movement can cause performance plateau due to an adaption of the central nervous system, resulting from a lack of stimulation.
